catalog_locator: Grammatical Outline, sec. 1.4 'Transition features and stress', points (b), (c) p. 189 and (g) p. 190 (PDF leaves 213-214 of)
catalog_quote: (b) Long and short vowels contrast only in the initial syllable of a phonological word, e.g. /kistan/ 'he pinched', /kīstan/ 'he scratched'. (c) In phonological words of two or more syllables, the first syllable is louder than the others, if it has a long vowel. On the other hand, if it has a short vowel, the second syllable is louder and is phonetically longer in quantity (though longer in open syllables, than in closed syllables). In both cases, all alternative syllables from the stressed ones carry a second degree loudness, and the rest of the syllables carry weak stress, e.g. /ūspazinad/ = [ú:s.pʌ.zǐ.nʌd] 'she is applying (oil) to herself'; /aṛbazinad/ = [ʌṛ.bá·.zɪ.nàd] 'she is crying'. ... (g) Insofar as the initial syllable is concerned, the feature of duration (short or long vowel) has a more dominant functional role than stress. An unstressed long vowel will not produce any ambi…

new_statements.quote: [sec. 2.4, pp. 58-60, from snippets, join marked ...] In Konda, short and long vowels contrast only in the initial syllable (Krishnamurti 1969: 188–92) of a 'phonological word'. ... A vowel in the first syllable is stressed if it is long; if it is short the second syllable is phonetically longer and louder and carries primary stress. All alternate syllables from the stressed one carry 'a second degree loudness' or prominence, [ús.pa.zì.nad] 'she is applying oil', [ar.bá.zi.nàd] 'she is crying'. A stop preceding a stressed vowel is markedly fortis. [p. 27, sec. 1.5.1, read held by the project] There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word, short or long.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-phonemic. Within the juncture-bounded phonological word, the first syllable is stressed if its vowel is long; if the first vowel is short, the second syllable takes primary stress and is phonetically lengthened and louder. Vowel length contrasts only in the initial syllable, so the rule amounts to: stress the long vowel if there is one, else the second syllable (left-edge two-syllable window, CVV heavy). Family-wide default stated in ch. 1 is initial stress, non-phonemic.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'All alternate syllables from the stressed one carry "a second degree loudness" or prominence' (alternating secondary stress counted from the primary), e.g. [ús.pa.zì.nad], [ar.bá.zi.nàd].
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Konda. The paragraph adds that a stop before a stressed vowel is markedly fortis, and (quoting 1969) that once word boundaries and initial-syllable length are marked, stress and length in the remaining syllables are 'automatic and predictable'; it also notes that a morphological word can be two phonological words (# nā + rāyna # 'Oh God!'), so the stress domain is the phonological, not the grammatical, word. The ch. 1 generalization ('normally stress falls on the initial syllable.. short or long') is a family-level default that the Konda-specific rule overrides when the initial vowel is short.
new_statements.identity_note: Both the catalog source (Krishnamurti 1969) and the 2003 restatement describe Konda/Kūbi as a single language; the 1969 snippet says the second-syllable accent in isolation is shared by 'all Konda (Kūbi) dialects including that of Guri', so no dialect restriction applies to the stress rule. The 2003 Konda paragraph is second-hand from the author's own 1969 grammar (cited as 1969: 188-92 and 1969a: 186-92), not a new description.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources. The only tension is internal to Krishnamurti 2003: the ch. 1 typological summary (p. 27) says stress 'normally' falls on the initial syllable in all Dravidian languages, short or long, while the Konda-specific paragraph in sec. 2.4 (following Krishnamurti 1969) says a short first syllable yields primary stress on the second syllable. The p. 27 sentence is an explicit family-wide default ('normally'), and the sec. 2.4 statement is the language-specific rule, so it is a refinement, not a contradiction; both the catalog (1969) and 2003 give the same Konda rule. A 1969 snippet surfaced by the same Google Books query ('All Konda (Kūbi) dialects including that of Guri sampled by me possess a common phonetic feature, viz., accenting the second syllable of a word when pronounced in isola[tion]') is consistent with the peninitial default across dialects.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim on the page images we hold (pp. 189-190, leaves 213-214). The deciding source is the standard fieldwork reference grammar (Krishnamurti 1969, 423 pp.), the only full grammar Glottolog lists, and its stress section is an explicit analysis with phonetic transcriptions that directly supports the 'weight' coding (CVV initial attracts stress; closed short-vowel initial does not, per /aṛbazinad/ [ʌṛ.bá·.zɪ.nàd]) and the alternating secondary. The book's Introduction (p. 23) independently notes second-syllable accent in isolation forms across dialects, consistent with the classification. No instrumental or later dedicated prosody study was found via CrossRef/archive. the only other descriptions are shorter sketches, two by the same author. Nothing suggests the classification would change.
